content:
To approve the reconfiguration and resurfacing
of Newmans Garden Car Park and the adjoining access road, including
the provision of a revised parking layout, additional disabled
parking bays and a one-way circulation system (‘the
works’).
 
To approve the appointment of a contractor to
undertake the works.
 
To approve the award of the required contract
(‘the contract’) to the contractor identified and at
the cost outlined in the exempt appendix.
 
To delegate authority to the Director of
Resources, in consultation with the Head of Legal and Democratic
Services, to finalise the terms and conditions of, and to approve
the entering into of, the contract.

The existing layout and condition of Newmans
Garden Car Park no longer meet current operational and
accessibility standards. The proposed scheme will provide parking
bays that comply with current design standards, increase the number
of disabled parking bays, improve vehicle circulation through the
introduction of a one-way system and renew the deteriorated
surfacing of both the car park and adjoining access road. Although
the overall number of parking spaces will be reduced, the scheme
represents the most effective use of the available space and will
improve safety, accessibility, customer experience and the
long-term condition of the asset. The contract has been procured in
accordance with the Council's procurement procedures and the
recommended contractor achieved the highest overall score through
the tender evaluation process, demonstrating the best combination
of price and quality.

Not to undertake the works.
This option was rejected due to the deteriorating condition of the
car park and access road surfacing, the number of undersized
parking bays and the inefficient vehicle circulation within the car
park.

None
topline: The Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Finance and Resources has decided to approve the reconfiguration and resurfacing of Newmans Garden Car Park and the adjoining access road.

content:
To approve the refreshed Horsham Growth Deal
2026–2030 (‘the Growth Deal’) (including the
action plan contained therein) between Horsham District Council
(‘HDC’) and West Sussex County Council
(‘WSCC’) as set out in Appendix A to the report.
 
To sign the Growth Deal together with the
Chief Executive on behalf of the Council.

The Growth Deal provides a
jointly agreed strategic framework between HDC and WSCC to align
investment, resources and delivery activity to support sustainable
economic growth across the District.
 
The Growth Deal:
 

Aligns with both
councils’ economic strategies and priorities
Establishes a clear
set of shared principles and governance arrangements
Identifies a
prioritised programme of projects to drive growth, regeneration and
infrastructure delivery
Strengthens the
Council’s ability to attract external funding and
investment

 
Approval of the Growth Deal
will enable continued collaboration with WSCC and partners,
maintaining momentum on key regeneration and infrastructure
projects and ensuring Horsham District is well positioned to
influence future regional funding and governance
arrangements.

1. Do
nothing / do not refresh the Growth Deal
 
Rejected as this would risk
loss of strategic alignment with WSCC, reduce the Council’s
ability to secure external funding, and weaken delivery momentum on
key growth and infrastructure projects.
 
2.
Develop a standalone HDC growth programme
 
Rejected as it would not
maximise the benefits of partnership working, shared investment,
and coordinated infrastructure delivery across the
county.

None
topline: The Leader of the Council has decided to approve the refreshed Horsham Growth Deal 2026-2030 between Horsham District Council and West Sussex County Council.

content:
RESOLVED
 
i)              
That the Horsham District Local Plan 2023-2040 Schedule of Proposed
Main Modifications as contained in Appendix 1, and updated policies
maps as set out in Appendix 2 of this report replacing the
published Inset Map 29 – Rusper
with the Inset Map 29 – Rusper
published as an addendum, together with the updated Sustainability
Appraisal, Habitats Regulations Assessment and other updated
evidence base documents for a 6 week period of representation from
Monday 13 July 2026 to Monday 24 August 2026 be approved.

 
ii)             
That authority be delegated to the Director of Place and Head of
Strategic Planning, in consultation with the Cabinet Member for
Planning and Infrastructure to modify the schedule of proposed main
modifications i) for the purpose of
correcting errors ii) to take account of any feedback or
correspondence provided by the Inspector in relation to the main
modification documentation.
 
iii)            
That is be noted that if the Planning Inspector recommends
modifications to the Local Plan under section 20(7C) of the
Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004, Cabinet will be asked to
modify the submission version of the Local Plan to incorporate
these modifications (along with any additional minor modifications)
and to recommend adoption of the Local Plan (as modified) to Full
Council.
 
 
REASONS
 
i)              
The recommendations are required to ensure that the Council meets
the statutory requirement to carry out a Local Plan review, and to
meet the requirements in the Town and County Planning (Local
Planning) (England) Regulations 2012.

 
ii)             
It is both legally necessary and appropriate to invite public and
stakeholder participation in the preparation of a new Local Plan
for Horsham District.
 
iii)            
To correct any typographical or factual errors, or to reflect
feedback or advice which may be received from the local plan
Inspector in connection with the Main Modifications, following the
publication of this cabinet report.
 
iv)            
To enable the Local Plan to continue to progress through
independent examination and accord with government requirements to
have an up-to-date local plan.
 
 
ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED BUT REJECTED AS
IDENTIFIED IN THE REPORT
 
An alternative option which is available to
the Council is to decide to withdraw this plan from examination and
commence planning under the new planning regulations. The impacts
of withdrawal of a plan were outlined in a paper considered by the
Communities and Place and Scrutiny committee on 23 July 2025.
Whilst the context of the discussion has changed, many of the key
risks remain and are highlighted below.
Withdrawal of the plan will leave the Council
in a position where it has no five-year housing supply against the
most recent standard housing methodology as set out in national
planning policy guidance. The Council will be at risk of
speculative development applications until a new plan is in place.
Whilst the Council has already commenced plan making under the new
planning regulations, it will not have an adopted plan in place for
nearly 3 years. This assumes plan making for the District is not complicated by Local Government
Reorganisation, which in the absence of any known geography for the
eventual unitary council, presents considerable uncertainties as to
how plan making may take place within any eventual unitary
authority.
 
Withdrawal of the plan was discounted because
it would undermine the Council’s ability to plan for growth
in a coordinated and sustainable way, increasing the risk of
unplanned and speculative development on unsuitable sites. This is
because the Council will no longer be able to attribute any weight
to the emerging policies within the Horsham District Local Plan
2023-2040, as it will cease to exist in formal terms. As the plan
is currently at examination, some weight can be afforded to the
emerging policies it contains. This weight will increase as the
plan progresses through the later hearings and on receipt of the
Inspector’s report. This will help guide and steer
development which does come forward. Conversely, unplanned
speculative development, some of which is expected to be at a
strategic scale, would impact on the District’s strategic and community
infrastructure. More development would come forward than that which
is set out in the proposed Main Modifications schedule, given the
continued inability of the Council to demonstrate it is meeting
government housing targets in any meaningful way. Further,
withdrawal of the plan also weakens the Council’s position in
decision-making and at appeal, making it harder to secure
infrastructure, protect valued landscapes and deliver strategic
priorities in line with the Council’s wider policy
framework.
 
At the Communities and Place Policy and
Scrutiny Committee on 23 July 2025, the implications of withdrawal
were considered so potentially damaging that an outcome of this
meeting was a request that the Director of Place write to the
Planning Inspectorate to ask them to reconsider their position in
view of the imminent changing planning regulations which would
repeal the Duty to Co-operate. Given this valuable Member feedback
which reflects the continued desire to have a local plan in place
as soon as possible, together with what would be considerable
reputational damage to the Council by withdrawal of the plan at
such a late stage, this course of action has been rejected.
 
It is a requirement that as part of plan
making, alternative plan options, including a range of different
site allocations are considered. This has been undertaken as part
of the Sustainability Appraisal, and of which further information
is set out in paragraphs 1.32 and 1.33. Not undertaking this work
was discounted as it is essential in ensuring that sites are
properly assessed and evidenced.
 
Not consulting on the proposed Main
Modifications was discounted given that the Local Plan Inspector
has requested that the Council does so
and the Council is required to do so in line with its policy
position and planning practice guidance.
 
As set out in paragraph 8.4 below, the Council
would also need to be mindful of any feedback on the Main
Modifications consultation that may be provided to the Council as
part of the ongoing examination process. The Council has discounted
the option of not actioning any advice or instruction provided by
the Inspector as this would either significantly delay or halt the
ongoing examination process.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve proposed main modifications to the Horsham District Local Plan 2023-2040 for a 6-week representation period.

content:
To approve the appointment of a contractor for
the design and build of South Holmes Play Area and Open Space
Renewal.
 
To approve the award of the required contract
(‘the contract’) to the contractor identified and at
the cost outlined in the exempt appendix.
 
To delegate authority to the Director of
Communities, in consultation with the Head of Legal and Democratic
Services, to finalise the terms and conditions of, and to approve
the entering into of, the contract.
 

South Holmes Play Area is
predominantly wooden, is very well used and is currently taking a
lot of regular maintenance to keep it going as it is over 26 years
old. It contains some large structures which need to be replaced
for safety. It is a key neighbourhood play area in Roffey South and
is located on the edge of Leechpool and Owlbeech Woods.
 
The main purposes of the renewal are to ensure
that the play area (1) meets required safety standards, (2) has
good play value, (3) provides activities and interest for children
of all abilities including children with disabilities and
neurodiverse children, and (4) provides opportunities for children
to experience controlled risk.
 
The benefits to the Council are (1) reduced
risk of accidents occurring on an older play area and (2)
reinforcing the Council’s reputation for providing good
quality, inclusive play facilities.
 
Renewal works will comprise the creation of a
natural play space that reflects the woodland environment and will
include the replacement of existing play equipment with new
improved equipment/features as well as new safety surfacing.
 

Do nothing and just patch up
the existing equipment and surfacing. This was rejected because (1)
given the age of the equipment there is increased risk of a failure
in the equipment resulting in an injury to a member of the public
and (2) the lack of investment in the play area means declining
visits by the public and an increase in anti-social
behaviour.
 
Other contractors were
considered but were rejected as part of the procurement
process.
 

None
topline: The Leader of the Council has decided to approve the appointment of a contractor for the renewal of South Holmes Play Area and Open Space.

content:
To approve the direct award of a contract for
the provision of AI apprenticeship training (‘the
contract’) for a term of two years to the supplier identified
and at the cost outlined in the exempt appendix.
 
To finalise the terms and conditions of and
enter into the contract in

 
The Chief Executive has considered the
available options and approves the direct award of a contract for
the provision of AI apprenticeship training. Market engagement
undertaken with potential providers concluded that the recommended
provider offers the strongest quality of provision, including
course content, delivery methodology, learner support and alignment
with organisational requirements. As apprenticeship training is
funded through the Apprenticeship Levy and providers operate within
prescribed funding bands, price was not a determining factor in the
evaluation. The decision is therefore based on the quality and
suitability of the training offer, with the recommended provider
representing the most advantageous option to support the
Council’s workforce development and AI skills objectives.

Undertake a competitive procurement exercise
to invite bids from training providers. 
This option was not recommended as soft market research had already
identified the preferred provider as offering the strongest quality
of provision.  Given that apprenticeship
training is funded through the Apprenticeship Levy and providers
charge against the same funding bands, a procurement exercise would
be unlikely to achieve any cost savings and would delay
implementation of the training programme.
 
Award the contract to an alternative
apprenticeship training provider.  This
option was considered but not recommended because market research
indicated that alternative providers did not offer the same level
of quality, course content, learner support, and alignment with
organisational requirements as the recommended
provider. 
 
Take no action and not procure AI
apprenticeship training.  This option
was rejected as it would limit opportunities to develop workforce
capability in AI.
 
 

None
topline: The Chief Executive has decided to approve the direct award of a contract for AI apprenticeship training to the recommended provider.

content:
RESOLVED – to review the
appropriateness:
 

      
i.        
Of a protocol for Ward Members who sit on Planning Committee to
support early engagement with developers in relation to
non-financial section 106 obligations, noting that the Monitoring
Officer is presently conducting a review of the Council’s
planning function;
 

    
ii.        
Of a policy providing for fall-back options and extended timescales
for the delivery of infrastructure (where appropriate) when
drafting non-financial section 106 planning obligations being
developed; 
 

   
iii.        
Of a process being established to facilitate engagement between
officers and local ward members when identifying heads of terms or
drafting non-financial section 106 planning obligations for
developments within their wards, noting that the Monitoring Officer
is presently conducting a review of the planning function;
 

   
iv.        
Of a review and, where appropriate, improvement to the way in which
non-financial section 106 planning obligations are displayed on the
planning portal to improve accessibility and transparency;
 

    
v.        
Of effective communication being encouraged between local ward
members and parish councils to discuss potential mitigation arising
from future developments in their area, noting that the Monitoring
Officer is presently undertaking a review of the Council’s
planning function; and
 

   
vi.        
Of Appendix B being submitted to Horsham District parish councils
as a good example of partnership working with developers and other
stakeholders, noting that the Monitoring Officer is presently
undertaking a review of the Council’s planning function.
 
REASONS
 

      
i.        
To ensure that any process for ward
member liaison with developers, in relation to S106 planning
obligations, is clear and transparent, allows ward members to
represent their constituents needs effectively, and where relevant,
enables them to remain effective members of the Planning
Committee.
 

    
ii.        
The inclusion of an extended time period for the provision of
infrastructure may assist in demonstrating the sustained need to
mitigate the impact of planning, thereby increasing the likelihood
that planned infrastructure is brought forward.
 

   
iii.        
In situations where a stakeholder, such as WSCC or NHS England,
have decided not to take up an option to provide infrastructure,
the inclusion of effective fall-back provisions in S106 planning
obligations may ensure that other routes to mitigate the impact of
planning can be explored.
 

   
iv.        
To ensure that S106 planning obligations are easily identifiable on
the planning portal, particularly when there have been variations
to the original agreement, to assist local ward members, parishes
and members of the public, who wish to monitor progress.
 
ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED BUT REJECTED AS
IDENTIFIED IN THE REPORT
 
Members could have kept within the original
terms of reference, but they considered their insight as ward
members could add value to initial discussions about nonfinancial
S106 planning obligations, both with developers, and with officers.
Whilst it was noted that a process had been put in place for
Members who did not sit on the Planning Committee, this was not in
place for those who did sit on Planning Committee.
 
Members are aware that the current planning
function is presently the subject of a formal review by the
Monitoring Officer. Given this, the Task and Finish Group
considered whether submission of an information report to the
Communities and Place Policy and Scrutiny Committee would be
appropriate. However, Members were keen to ensure that the
potential improvements they had identified were actively taken
forward for consideration. They concluded that this could only be
achieved by submitting formal recommendations.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to review and potentially improve protocols, policies, processes, and communication related to non-financial section 106 planning obligations.

content:
RESOLVED
 
i)              
That the West Chiltington Neighbourhood Plan (2023 - 2031) as part
of the statutory development plan for Horsham District be formally
made; and

 
ii)             
That authority be delegated to the Director of Place, in
consultation with the Cabinet Member for Planning and
Infrastructure and with the consent of West Chiltington Parish
Council, to modify the West Chiltington Neighbourhood Plan
(i) for the purpose of correcting
errors and/or (ii) if the modification does not materially affect
the policies in the plan.
 
REASONS
 
i)              
To meet the requirements of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase
Act 2004 and the Neighbourhood Planning (General) Regulations
2012.

 
ii)             
To enable corrections and non-material modifications to be made to
the plan in a timely manner, to ensure the accuracy and
effectiveness of the plan.
 
ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED BUT REJECTED AS
IDENITIFIED IN THE REPORT
 
The Council can decide not to make the West
Chiltington Neighbourhood Plan if it considers that doing so would
breach, or would otherwise be incompatible with, an assimilated
obligation (previously known as retained EU law) or any of the
Convention rights within the meaning of the Human Rights Act 1998.
Having taken into account the views of the examiner and having
regard to the wider legal implications set out in section 8 of this
report, it is not considered that this is the case. The Council is
therefore required to make the plan.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to formally make the West Chiltington Neighbourhood Plan and delegate authority for modifications.

content:
To approve the reconfiguration of Jengers Mead Car Park (‘the Car Park’)
to reduce the number of available parking spaces from 17 to 10 as
shown in Appendix 1 to this report
 
To approve the necessary works to reconfigure
the Car Park and to delegate authority to the Head of Parking and
Enterprise to authorise such works
 
To approve the variation of
the Horsham District
Council (Off-Street Parking Places) (Consolidation) Order 2023
to reflect the reconfiguration of the Car Park and to delegate
authority to the Head of Legal and Democratic Services to make the
variation order subject to no objections being received during the
consultation process

It has come to light that part
of the existing car park falls outside of the Council’s land
ownership. Acceptable terms could not be agreed with the
third-party landowner to enable continued use of this
section.
 
The proposed reconfiguration
allows the Council to continue operating the car park within the
confines of its land ownership, ensuring ongoing provision of
parking while avoiding ongoing financial liabilities.

To enter into an agreement with
the third-party landowner to retain use of the affected section of
land. This option was rejected as the financial terms proposed were
considered unsuitable and did not represent value for money,
particularly given the limited income generated by the car
park.

None
topline: The Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Finance and Resources has decided to reconfigure Jengers Mead Car Park, reducing parking spaces from 17 to 10.

To approve the “notice of
scoping consultation” (Appendix C) and to authorise that it
be published and made available for inspection;

 

To delegate authority to the
Director of Place, in consultation with the Cabinet Member for
Planning and Infrastructure, to prepare, approve, publish and make
available for inspection (i) a “self-assessment
summary” and (ii) a “summary of scoping
consultation”; and

 

  
ix.       
To delegate authority to the Head of Strategic
Planning, in consultation with the Director of Place and the
Cabinet Member for Planning and Infrastructure as necessary, to
take such further steps as may be required to give effect to and
progress the preparation of Horsham District 2045.
 


It is a legal requirement to
commence work on a local plan under the new plan-making system by
the 30 June 2026.

 

Local Planning Authorities are under
a legal duty to prepare and maintain a timetable setting out the
timeline for the preparation of planning documents and passing
through gateways. For HDC this deadline is 30 June 2026.

 

Under new regulations, it is a
requirement to update the timetable at least monthly. Delegation is
necessary to ensure this can be met in a timely manner.

 

Under new regulations, it is a
requirement to hold an initial scoping consultation prior to
commencement of plan-making.

 

Under new regulations, it is a
requirement to publish the self-assessment summary to proceed
through Gateway 1 of the new planning system and to publish the
summary of scoping consultation detailing feedback received.

 

The alternative course of action would be to
not begin work on a plan under the new plan-making system. However,
this has been rejected as it would result in a breach of
regulations and may result in the Secretary of State intervening to
begin plan preparation.
 

None

content:
To approve the Local Code of Governance
(“the Code”).
 
To delegate authority to the Director of
Resources to update the Code annually, in consultation with the
Leader of the Council and having regard to the views of the Audit
Committee.

The Chartered Institute of Public Finance and
Accountancy (“CIPFA”) published an addendum to its
document “Delivering Good Governance in Local Government:
Framework” in May 2025.The addendum states that “CIPFA
and Solace recommend that authorities adopt a local code of
governance which sets out their governance arrangements, showing
how governance principles are put into practice at their
authority”.
 
The addendum recommends that local authorities
adopt a more comprehensive local code of governance than before to
provide stronger evidence of their alignment to good governance
principles. The Council’s code has been rewritten to reflect
the guidance contained in the addendum.
 
It is good practice for a local code of
governance to be reviewed and updated regularly.

To not have a local code of governance. If the
Council does not have a local code of governance, the annual review
of governance which takes place prior to the Annual Governance
Statement being prepared would first need to identify the
arrangements in place to meet good governance principles.
Therefore, not having a code would impact the annual governance
review and the Annual Governance Statement, and so was
rejected.
 
To continue to use the existing local code of
governance. This was rejected in favour of creating a more
comprehensive and accessible code, aligned with the addendum, to
better support the annual governance review.

No conflicts have been declared.
topline: The Leader of the Council has decided to approve a new Local Code of Governance in alignment with CIPFA's recommendations.

content:
The decision to appoint a new supplier to

The current asset management system had not
been market tested for some years and with the rising cost of the
service and its lack of compatibility with internal and external
GiS systems was leading to poor data quality which was not meeting
the needs of the service.
 
The extant service agreement with the current
supplier did not meet the requirements of procurement legislation.
A more formal agreement is required and has been put in place
through this exercise.
 
The procurement exercise identified multiple
alternatives which more closely met the essential and desired
criteria established by the department. 
The current supplier did not meet essential criteria.
 
The selected supplier’s software met all
criteria and will improve service delivery at a lower annual price
point.

Staying with the existing provider was not an
option as it was failing to meet our service requirements and had
been on a rolling annual licence for a number of years without
being reviewed.
 
We undertook a G-Cloud based procurement
exercise in which we considered all suppliers within that
framework.  Other software suppliers are
available but are not within our framework.

None.

content:
RESOLVED
 
i)             
To place Horsham Park into the Fields in Trust scheme by entering
into a Deed dedicating the park as a public playing field,
recreation ground, park, play space and open space;

 
ii)            
That responsibility be delegated to sign the Deed to the Director
of Communities, in consultation with the Head of Legal and
Democratic Services; and
 
iii)          
To authorise the Head of Legal and Democratic Services, in
consultation with the Director of Communities to make amendments to
the Deed of Dedication following final negotiations with Fields in
Trust.
 
REASON
 
To enable the Council to deliver in its
previously stated objective to place Horsham Park into the Fields
in Trust scheme.
 
ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED BUT REJECTED AS
IDENTIFIED IN THE REPORT
 
i)             
Do nothing. This was discounted on the basis that placing the park
into the Fields in Trust scheme represents the Council’s
desire to dedicate it for community use;
 
ii)            
Designate Horsham Park as a Town/Village Green. While offering very
strong statutory protection, this was discounted on the basis that
such a designation may prove to be extremely inflexible and block
improvements;
 
iii)          
Designate the park as a Local Green Space, through the planning
system. While offering green belt level planning protection, this
was discounted on the basis that the Park benefits already from
existing planning protections (for example, it has been identified
as a Green Infrastructure Asset in the Infrastructure Strategy, a
multi-functional green space in the Open Space Assessment and is
protected under the Horsham Blueprint Neighbourhood Plan for
recreation and community use. Additionally, the Council’s
existing and emerging Local Plans and National Planning Policy
Framework seek to prevent the loss of the Park ) and such a
designation relies on planning policy which can change over
time;
 
iv)          
Move the land into an independent or charitable trust. This was
discounted on the basis that it may be difficult to recruit
trustees and the transfer of the park into a trust would likely
require Secretary of State consent.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to dedicate Horsham Park for community use by placing it into the Fields in Trust scheme.

1990 to formulate and publish proposals for preserving and
enhancing conservation areas. In addition, it was considered that
to not undertake the review would risk the impact of development
(in or nearby this sensitive location) not adequately considering
or taking account of the special historic and architectural
character of the conservation area. This would limit the
Council’s ability to manage change in a positive way.

content:
RESOLVED
 
i)             
The affordable housing scheme comprising nine residential units at
the Council owned Dukes Square site (“the Scheme”) be
approved.

 
ii)            
The (i) transfer of Section 106 funds the value of which is
contained in the exempt appendix 1 to Horsham District Homes

A loan to Horsham District Homes Limited in the sum of up the value
of which is detailed in the exempt appendix to construct the
affordable homes, adding this to the capital programme and
delegating to the Director of Resources to profile this loan into
the 2026/27 and 2027/28 capital programme when the lead times are
known be approved
 
iv)          
That authority be delegated to the Director of Place to enter into
the various associated contracts and other agreements/deeds to
facilitate the delivery of the Scheme
 
v)           
To (a) determine that the Dukes Square site is no longer required
for garage use, (b) approve the appropriation of the Dukes Square
site from a garage site to planning purposes, and, (c) approve that
the Council may rely on section 203 of the Housing and Planning Act
1990 to override easements and other rights in the Duke Square
Site, subject to payment of compensation under section 204 of that
Act, if applicable.
 
vi)          
To approve, if required, (a) the award of any contracts to the
successful bidder required to give effect to the delivery of the
Scheme, and, (b) the delegation of authority to the Director of
Place in consultation with the Head of Legal and Democratic
Services to finalise the terms of and enter into any contracts
required to give effect to the delivery of the Scheme.
 
vii)         
That authority be delegated to the Director of Place in
consultation with the Head of Legal and Democratic Services to take
all necessary actions to give effect to the delivery and
implementation of the Scheme (including seeking, amongst other
things, a covenant and indemnity from its housing companies to
abide by the terms of a restriction in favour of the Ministry of
Defence).
 
viii)        
The freehold transfer of the Dukes Square Site to Horsham District
Homes Limited for best value be approved.
 
 
REASONS
 
i)             
This site has planning approval for nine homes. The development of
affordable housing aligns with the restriction by the Ministry of
Defence to provide accommodation for those with a housing need.
ii)            
This is a key decision.
iii)          
To ensure the delivery of the Scheme, an appropriate structure is
in place, the allocation of funds, the appropriation of the Dukes
Square site (along with overriding any rights) and the award of
relevant contracts, where required.
 
 
ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED BUT REJECTED AS
IDENTIFIED IN THE REPORT
 
Development of market housing was rejected
owing to the existence of the restriction on the Dukes Square and
that there is a public need for affordable homes.
 
Converting the premises to a permanent storage
use was rejected due to the deteriorating condition of the Asbestos
cladding on the building, making it not fit for long term use, the
reduction in demand for garage use and the fact that the affordable
housing need outweighs the retention of the garages.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve an affordable housing scheme at the Dukes Square site, including the transfer of funds and land appropriation.

decision_maker: Cabinet Member for Wellbeing, Culture and Green Spaces
content:
To approve the appointment of a contractor for
the supply and construction of improvements to a section of a path
in Horsham Park.
 
To approve the award of the required contract
(‘the contract’) to the contractor identified and at
the cost outlined in the exempt appendix.
 
To delegate authority to the Director of
Communities, in consultation with the Head of Legal and Democratic
Services, to finalise the terms and conditions of, and to approve
the entering into of, the contract.
 

The existing path is narrow at 1.3m and does not
provide sufficient width for users, particularly in winter. The
improvements will include widening a section of existing path and
creating a new path with overall widths of 2.75m.
 
The main purposes of the
improvements are (i) to allow multiple recreational uses at the
same time (to include runners, dog walkers, cyclists, groups of
pedestrians) by increasing the width of the path and (ii) to
improve safety by re-routing the path away from the wooded
perimeter.
 
The works will improve access
to a well-used route across the park for all users. Students from
the College of Richard Collyer in Hurst Road use this route
regularly in large groups and will especially benefit from the
improvements.
 

No improvements carried out to the path. This
was rejected because improvements are required for the reasons
outlined above.
 
Other contractors were considered as part of
the procurement process but were rejected as they were more
expensive.
 

None
topline: The Cabinet Member for Wellbeing, Culture and Green Spaces has decided to approve the appointment of a contractor for improvements to a section of a path in Horsham Park

decision_maker: Cabinet Member for Planning and Infrastructure
content:
To
approve the direct award of a contract for the provision of a
cloud-based planning system (‘the contract’) for a term
of five years to the supplier identified and at the cost outlined
in  the exempt appendix.
 
To
delegate authority to the Director of Place, in consultation with
the Head of Legal and Democratic Services, to finalise the terms
and conditions of, and to approve the entering into of, the contract.
 

Moving to a cloud-based system will give the Council increased
benefits in terms of workload management and performance management
for managers as well as
giving planners access to onsite capabilities.
 
The
proposed supplier is the market leader and several local
authorities across West Sussex are already using their system for
planning and some are already upgrading to their cloud-based
system.
 
The
decision to move to a cloud-based system also aligns with the
Council’s Digital and Technology Strategy, reducing the risk
of the inability to access planning systems. The planning system is
the single largest digital system the Council has, which holds
approximately 2 million records. It is the biggest IT risk system
in the Council as it is based on the premises, therefore having the
cloud-based solution in place would remove this risk.
 
There are also significant cost savings with a move to the
cloud-based system.
 

To
continue with the Council’s current planning system. This was
rejected as it would mean that the Council’s annual costs
would continue to increase to allow for upgrades and maintenance.
(This was detailed in a paper written for the Council’s
Senior Leadership Team (‘SLT’) as well as further
detail on proposed costs sitting within existing
budgets).  There is also no future
development proposed for the current system.
 

None.
topline: The Cabinet Member for Planning and Infrastructure has decided to approve a contract for a cloud-based planning system.

content:
To approve the purchase of 1 x Electric Maxus

content:
To revoke the Cowfold Air Quality Management
Area.

The
Council declared “Cowfold Air
Quality Management Area”
an
Air Quality Management Area (AQMA) in 2011 due to
measured exceedances of the annual mean nitrogen
dioxide
(NO2) air quality
objective.
 
The
Council has been monitoring NO2 in Cowfold since 2008.
Currently, there are nine diffusion tubes in Cowfold, of which
five are within the AQMA. There has been no exceedance
of
the
objectives since 2020 and concentrations in 2019 were
only
marginally over 10% of the annual mean NO2 objective
(36.1
?g/m3). The Council is
satisfied that the objectives will continue
to
be met at all locations in the future and proposed to
revoke
the
AQMA in its 2025 Air Quality Annual Status Report (ASR).
DEFRA has also confirmed that the Council must revoke
the
AQMA.

Not
to revoke the Horsham Cowfold AQMA.
This was rejected
in
order to comply with paragraph 3.61 of the Local Air
Quality
Management Technical Guidance (TG22) issued by DEFRA
in
May
2025 which states that there “should not
be any declared
AQMAs for which compliance with the relevant objective
has
been achieved for a consecutive five-year period”.
This was
reiterated by DEFRA in its
appraisal of the Council’s 2025 ASR.

N/A
topline: The Director of Communities has decided to revoke the Cowfold Air Quality Management Area due to improved air quality levels.

and relieving homelessness, the Strategy also addresses the need to
provide affordable homes to meet local need.

The Strategy is aligned with the objectives of the Council’s
Annual Plan, Local Plan, and relevant legislation, such as the
Homelessness Reduction Act 2017 and the Homes England Social and
Affordable Homes Programme.

Homelessness Strategy is due to expire in 2026. Due to the
statutory requirement to publish a Homelessness Strategy every five
years, the Council would not be fulfilling its statutory
obligations if the current Strategy was not replaced.

(i) Full Council approval of the
associated budgets, and (ii) the satisfactory conclusion of legal
due diligence related to these proposals):
 
(i)            
To approve the refurbishment of the Premises by the Council in the
sum of £900,000; 

 
(ii)           
To approve the provision of a contribution in the sum of
£175,000 to the Tenant to facilitate their fit-out works;
 
(iii)          
To approve a procurement exemption allowing the Council to obtain
quotes or utilise a framework to employ a contractor to carry out
the refurbishment works, rather than conducting a formal open
tender process; and
 
(iv)          
To approve entering into any documentation required to give effect
to the recommendations contained in this report, and, delegate
authority to the Head of Legal and Democratic Services
(i) to finalise the terms of and enter
into any required documentation to give effect to the above
recommendations, and, (ii) to undertake any functions required to
enable related legal due diligence to be concluded to ensure the
viability of the proposals contained within these
recommendations. 
 
 
REASONS
 
To facilitate the refurbishment and associated
leasing of the Premises.
 
ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED BUT REJECTED AS
IDENTIFIED IN THE REPORT
 
Other leisure operators were considered,
however, the proposed tenant presented the most favourable
combination of ideal property use, strong financial covenant,
significant investment commitment and competitive rental offer.
Their proposal stands out as the best option for ensuring the
long-term success and viability of the Premises.
 
The option of using the Premises for a social
purpose was carefully considered but ultimately rejected, as the
income generated from such use would be significantly lower
compared to leasing the Premises to a commercial leisure operator.
Leasing to a commercial operator offers a far more sustainable and
profitable revenue stream, ensuring both the financial viability of
the Premises, the long-term benefit to the Council and brings about
benefits for the community in terms of an additional leisure
offering.  
The option of demolishing the Premises and
rebuilding as a purpose-built leisure facility, such as a Padel
court facility,was considered but
rejected, as the Premises if refurbished ensures the asset value is
preserved. Furthermore, it would be more timely to instigate and
other operators would more readily provide the leisure options
throughout the district.

content:
To approve a revised community and voluntary
sector grants framework that transitions from the “strategic
grants model” to a rolling programme of unrestricted funding
of up to £15,000 for each application per financial year.
 

The process was reviewed in
2024 to make it easier for organisations to apply for funding based
on their needs and to ensure that HDC funding is used efficiently.
HDC’s strategic grants were available to organisations once a
year but were largely requests for year-on-year funding and not
strategic in nature and most of these were for small amounts.
Organisations can now apply for a grant of up to £15k in any
year.
 

To move back towards the
strategic grant process. However, this was an inflexible
arrangement as organisations had to apply the previous year and
very little funding was left for other, often smaller groups. With
the new arrangement, organisations can apply for funding for up to
£15,000 for both core costs and for projects during one of
our four grant rounds throughout the year.

To approve a one-year contract for Citizens
Advice West Sussex (CAWS) to deliver a dedicated outreach service
to assist residents who are struggling financially to maximise
their income by identifying relevant welfare benefits and provide a
holistic needs assessment.
 
To delegate authority to the Director of
Communities, in consultation with the Head of Legal and Democratic
Services, to finalise the terms and conditions of, and to approve
the entering into of the contract.
 

Although Horsham is a relatively
affluent area, there are many residents across the
District that
are struggling financially and are unaware of their benefit
entitlements. CAWS can address this gap by providing a holistic
assessment of the needs of users including those on a low income
and maximise their outcomes by identifying the welfare benefits
they are entitled to and provide support to access and receive the
correct entitlements.
 

Horsham District Council (HDC)
previously funded a similar contract with CAWS through the purchase
of a database which identified vulnerable households (LIFT).
Continuation of LIFT would not be a cost-effective use of resources
as there will be an additional cost of around £40k a year for
the database and many of the households listed have already been
targeted. It is felt that an outreach service, delivered in
locations where access to services is a barrier would be a more
cost-effective way of reaching additional vulnerable
households.
 

None

content:
To increase the annual subscription fee for
the Council’s Garden waste collection service by £5
from £59 to £64 per bin.
 

Local authorities are required to provide a
garden waste collection to residents who request it and are
permitted to charge for doing so. The Council proposes to increase
the annual subscription fee for its garden waste collection service
by £5 per bin in order
to maintain a cost-efficient
service.
 

To continue at the current price, raise the
price by £2 per bin or by £5.50 per bin. These options
were rejected because We wanted to ensure that the rise is kept as
low as possible so rejected the £5.50 but needed this to be
higher than the £2 per bin because the increase is necessary
to ensure the continued delivery of this high-quality service
without compromising our standards. Without this increase
we’re at risk of underfunding this service given inflation,
higher energy prices and staffing costs so this reflects the actual
cost pressures we face. This will keep the service financially
sustainable and remains proportionate in comparison to other local
authority prices.

None
topline: The Cabinet Member for Environmental Health, Recycling and Waste has decided to increase the annual subscription fee for the Council's Garden waste collection service by £5 per bin.

Councillor James Brookes, Chairman of
Governance Committee, introduced the item and moved the
recommendations. The Council were provided with an overview of the
community governance review process, including the consultations
that had taken place. Residents of the unparished area had
indicated support for the creation of a parish council, as well as
the relevant district and county councillors, the Member of
Parliament for Horsham and the Neighbourhood Councils. West Sussex
County Council stated that they did not oppose the creation of a
parish council in principle, but queried the timing of the review,
indicated that a referendum should be held, and that the boundary
of the parish should be considered in relation to the entire area
of the urban settlement. The neighbourhood councils were thanked
for their exceptional work over the last 50 years.
 
Members spoke in support of the proposals and
highlighted the importance of ensuring democratic representation
and local decision making, particularly in the context of local
government reorganisation. It was felt that the creation of a
parish council would safeguard the interests of the town and would
benefit residents and those who work in the town, through the
provision of facilities and services. The Leader recognised that
residents had concerns in relation to the cost of having a parish
council. The precept for a Band D property was anticipated at
£15 and the implication of this cost was taken seriously.
This consideration was balanced against the important role the
parish council would have as local government undergoes
reorganisation.
 
The Committee acknowledged the valuable role
previously played by neighbourhood councils in the unparished area
and expressed thanks to all who had contributed to the
consultation.
 
Councillor Alex Jeffery stated that the
creation would ensure that there was an authority in place with
statutory powers to protect the interests of residents in Horsham
town. He seconded the motion and spoke in support.
 
RESOLVED
 
i)     
That a budget of £45,000 in 2025/26 be allocated to the
set-up costs
 
ii)    
That the Horsham District Council (Reorganisation of Community
Governance) Order 2025 (‘the Reorganisation Order’), as
attached in draft form at Appendix 5 to this report, be made to (i)
give effect to the above recommendations and (ii) establish an
interim body (‘the Shadow Horsham Parish Council’) for
the purposes of preparing for the establishment of the new parish
council;  
 
iii)  
That authority be delegated individually or collectively to the
Chief Executive, the Director of Resources, the Head of Legal and
Democratic Services and the Democratic Services and Elections
Manager to take any action necessary to conclude the Community
Governance Review in accordance with legislation and statutory
guidance and to secure the implementation of the final
recommendations of the review as set out in the draft
Reorganisation Order; and
 
iv)  
That authority be delegated individually or collectively to the
Chief Executive, the Director of Resources, the Head of Legal and
Democratic Services and the Democratic Services and Elections
Manager, in consultation with the Leader of the Council and the
Chair of the Shadow Horsham Parish Council (if so appointed), to
take any action necessary for the effective implementation of the
new parish council.
 
REASONS
 
i)     
The making of a reorganisation order is a function of Full Council,
per “Functions of the Full Council” of the
Constitution. 
 
ii)    
Full Council must approve the revenue budget required.
topline: The Council has decided to create a parish council in an unparished area, allocating a budget of £45,000 for set-up costs.

content:
RESOLVED
 
i)              
The changes detailed in this report in the Council’s
financial position in 2025/26 and medium-term financial strategy
were noted

 
ii)             
Subject to recommendation iii), approve that the Council remains in
the West Sussex Business Rates pool in 2026/27 and to delegate
authority to the Director of Resources in consultation with the
Cabinet Member for Finance and Resources to (a) agree the
operational details of the pooling arrangements with participating
authorities, and, (b) enter into any required documentation to give
effect to this proposal.
 
iii)            
Authority was delegated to the Director of Resources in
consultation with the Cabinet Member for Finance and Resources to
withdraw from the West Sussex Business Rates pool for 2026/27
should the robust modelling undertaken once the Provisional
Settlement is announced and the details of the business rates reset
are known result in an unfavourable outcome for the Council in his
opinion.
 
 
REASONS
 
i)              
The Council needs to acknowledge the effects that inflation, cost
growth and reduced income will have on its financial position both
in the short and mediumterm. Deficits
are predicted in the medium-term unless action is taken on fees and
charges, and savings are made. Given the level of uncertainty in
the projections, the economy and proposed Government action, the
report does not recommend direct action to drastically reduce
expenditure but does recommend the need to consider decisions like
these when setting the 2026/27 budget in January 2026, should the
Provisional Settlement in December 2025 be more unfavourable.

 
ii)             
Having a West Sussex Business Rates pool should benefit the County
and therefore the district by retaining locally generated business
rates, using it to further support the economic regeneration of the
wider West Sussex area. However, there is a significant risk in the
context of Fair Funding and Business Rates reset that the modelling
may not be favourable if continuing with a pool.
 
ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED BUT REJECTED AS
IDENTIFIED IN THE REPORT
 
Making wholesale cuts to popular non-statutory
services such as Parks and Countryside, planning enforcement and
cultural and leisure services were considered. This was rejected
because the scale of the proposed deficits in the future is very
uncertain. While designed to protect services, this approach does
risk the Council having greater difficulties balancing its
financial position in the future and this will have an impact on
reserves, unless income is increased through fees and charges
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Council's participation in the West Sussex Business Rates pool for 2026/27, with the option to withdraw if financial modeling indicates a negative outcome.

RESOLVED
 
Approved the adoption of, with no changes to,
the existing modified scheme under Housing Benefit subsidy for
2026/27 whereby the Council locally and voluntarily disregards war
disablement pensions and war widow pensions in the Housing Benefit
calculation.
 
REASON
 
The locally modified Housing Benefit scheme is
an annual scheme requiring an annual review and approval, even when
no changes to the scheme are being proposed. The scheme remains
affordable for Horsham District Council and provides a good level
of support to our less well-off residents.
 
ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED BUT REJECTED AS
IDENTIFIED IN THE REPORT
 
Horsham District Council has the authority to
do nothing and keep the scheme the same as it is now or reduce the
amount of financial support awarded through this scheme. However,
the latter course of action was rejected because of the need to
continue to support the financially vulnerable.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the adoption of a modified Housing Benefit scheme for 2026/27, maintaining support for financially vulnerable residents.

RESOLVED
 
i)              
The conversion of the Old Ambulance Station (‘the
premises’) into a workshop to be used primarily for servicing
food waste vehicles (‘the workshop’) be approved;

 
ii)             
That authority be delegated to the Director of Resources to apply
for any relevant grant funding to be used towards the costs of
converting the premises;
 
iii)            
That authority be delegated to the Director of Place in
consultation with the Cabinet Member for Enterprise and Property to
approve the final designs for the workshop;
 
iv)            
The award of any contracts required to give effect to the
conversion of the premises and the acquisition and installation of
all required equipment (including an additional workshop van) be
approved; and
 
v)             
That authority be delegated to the Director of Place in
consultation with the Head of Legal and Democratic Services to
finalise the terms and conditions of, and to approve the entering
into of, any contracts or other
documentation required to give effect to the conversion of the
premises and the acquisition and installation of the required
equipment.
 
RECOMMENDED TO COUNCIL
 
i)              
To approve a capital budget of up to £488,000 for the 2025/26
financial year for the conversion of the premises and the
acquisition and installation of the required equipment, to be
funded from the Food Waste earmarked reserve; and

 
ii)             
To approve a revenue budget of £17,585 for the 2025/26
financial year to cover the running costs of the workshop and the
loss of income from the tenant for the last quarter of the
financial year, to be funded from the Food Waste earmarked
reserve.
 
REASONS
 
i)              
A new workshop is required to service and maintain the additional
vehicles procured for domestic food waste collections commencing in
March 2026. Following assessment, the Property Team has identified
the conversion of a Council-owned premises as the most suitable of
5 options that were assessed.

 
ii)             
Full Council must approve capital and revenue budgets.
 
 
ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED BUT REJECTED AS
IDENTIFIED IN THE REPORT
 

i)     
There are insufficient facilities to service the new vehicles in
the existing depot and insufficient space for it to be extended,
even if hours of operation are increased.
 

ii)    
A premises was briefly available at £55,000 per annum, but
the Property Team were unable secure it or find another premises
with the required height or with an existing maintenance pit.
 

iii)   
An existing tenant was potentially closing their business, meaning
a premises in Southwater Business Park would have been available.
However, the rental foregone would have been £35,000 per
annum and the tenant subsequently decided to carry on and remain in
the property.
 

iv)   
It is unsustainable to put the vehicles out to contract
maintenance. Outsourcing costs have been put together based on a
quote received for the work which would be required. It is
estimated that there would be an annual cost of £185,000 to
maintain the 15 vehicles. This would be an ongoing annual cost and
is likely to increase as the vehicles age. Additionally, vehicles
will need to be moved to and from third party workshops which adds
time onto the servicing and maintenance and means we lose control
of managing timescales for the vehicles to be back in use
topline: The Cabinet and Council have decided to convert the Old Ambulance Station into a workshop for servicing food waste vehicles.

content:
To approve the entering into of a contract for
the installation of a new CCTV system at the Forum car park,
together with associated maintenance for a period of three years,
to the supplier identified and at the cost outlined in the exempt
appendix.
 

The Forum car park has
experienced a prolonged period of vandalism, anti-social behaviour
and disturbances affecting both the car park and neighbouring
residential areas. A recent multi-agency meeting identified that
existing CCTV coverage in and around the site was inadequate, with
several cameras inoperable and key areas not monitored. As a
result, Police and Council wardens were unable to target patrols
effectively, and persistent offenders could not be reliably
identified. Evidence retrieval from the remaining CCTV system was
also time-consuming, often taking several hours to
compile.
 
The installation of a new CCTV
system is therefore necessary to strengthen community safety and
enable a more effective operational response. The upgraded system
will provide modern, high-quality coverage of the areas where
incidents most frequently occur and will significantly improve
officers’ ability to identify repeat offenders and accurately
determine the timing and nature of incidents within minutes. The
technology will also generate real-time alerts when groups gather
in known problem locations, allowing Police and warden patrols to
be deployed in a more targeted, intelligence-led manner.
 
The new system will provide a
combination of deterrent, proactive and reactive benefits:
deterring potential offenders through visible, modern CCTV;
enabling proactive early intervention through live alerts; and
improving reactive capabilities by providing rapid access to
evidential footage. Together, these improvements are expected to
substantially reduce ongoing incidents of vandalism and anti-social
behaviour and enhance safety for car park users and nearby
residents.
 

1. Increased Police and Warden Patrols
(Rejected):

While additional patrols were
considered, both Police and Council wardens reported that without
reliable CCTV coverage they were unable to target activity
effectively or identify persistent offenders. Patrol-only
approaches would not address the core issue of poor situational
awareness and would continue to rely on reactive responses rather
than prevention.
 
2. Repairing or Maintaining the Existing
CCTV System (Rejected):

The current system has multiple
inoperable cameras and does not provide adequate coverage of key
areas where incidents are occurring. Simply repairing or
maintaining the outdated equipment would not deliver the
technological capability needed to identify offenders quickly,
receive real-time alerts, or retrieve evidence
efficiently.
 
3. Installing Fewer Cameras or a
Reduced-Specification System (Rejected):

A scaled-down system was
assessed but would not provide sufficient visibility of the known
problem areas or the advanced functionality required for
intelligence-led patrols. This would limit both deterrence and
evidential value, resulting in only marginal improvement over the
current situation.
 
4. Maintaining the
Status Quo (Rejected):

Leaving the current arrangements unchanged would allow ongoing
vandalism and anti-social behaviour to continue, with no practical
means to identify perpetrators or reduce incidents. This option
would not address community safety concerns raised by residents,
Police, and partner agencies.
 

N/A
topline: The Head of Parking & Enterprise has decided to approve the installation of a new CCTV system at the Forum car park to address vandalism and anti-social behaviour issues.

To approve the purchase of 1 x electric
powered Luton van with tail lift for the Council’s bulky
waste service at a cost of £57,000.
 
To approve the award of the required purchase
contract to the supplier selected pursuant to the relevant
framework agreement (‘the contract’).
 
To finalise the terms and conditions of and
enter into the contract in consultation with the Head of Legal and
Democratic Services.

The existing vehicle is now due for scheduled
replacement as it has come to the end of its useful economic life.
This vehicle also has a clutch problem that is likely to cost
£2,000 to repair and it is considered better value to
purchase a new van than to repair the old one.
 
The cost of the vehicle is £57,000. This
vehicle is on the capital replacement plan for the 2025/26
financial year.

HVO powered options were considered, but this
is not in keeping with the Council’s agenda to become carbon
neutral. Having both types of vehicles on the fleet, we have now
assessed that the electric version have lower running costs that
will pay back against the higher capital cost. For instance, to
fill an HVO version would cost £71 compared to a full charge
that would cost £30.
 
Hiring a replacement vehicle at £390 per
week was rejected on cost grounds.
 
To carry on using the current vehicle and risk
overspending on the budget for maintenance.

None
topline: The Director of Communities has decided to approve the purchase of a new electric-powered Luton van for the Council's bulky waste service.

content:
(i)           
To appropriate the dwellinghouse and curtilage referred to and
shown edged in red on the plan contained in the exempt appendix
(“the Property”) from its current use by the Council in
its function as a burial authority to general housing accommodation
for persons with special needs under section 122 of the Local
Government Act 1972 with effect from the date of this decision;
and
(ii)          
To authorise the granting of a lease of the Property by the Council
to the Council’s housing company Horsham District Homes
(Holdings) Limited for a term of five years at an affordable
rent.
 

The Property is held by the Council for the
purpose of discharging the Council’s function as a burial
authority. The Property is considered to have been residential in
use save for a short period of temporary office use. Save for one
small building situated at the rear of the Property which will
continue to be used by the Council in connection with its function
as a burial authority, the Property itself is no longer required
for this purpose and works were authorised to adapt the house and
grounds of the Property for persons with special needs. Planning
permission was granted for such works
and the Council therefore wishes to appropriate the Property to use
the same as general housing accommodation for persons with special
needs.
 
As the Council is a local housing authority
and discharges its housing function through the Council’s
housing company Horsham District Homes (Holdings) Limited, the
Council will grant a lease of the Property to the housing company
for a term of five years at an affordable rent. This company will
then manage and let out the Property as housing accommodation for
persons with special needs on an assured shorthold tenancy
basis.
 

Consideration has been given to different
options for the Property, which include the following:
(a) 
incorporating it into the Temporary Housing Portfolio;
(b) 
disposing of it on the open market; or
(c)  
letting it on an assured shorthold tenancy at an affordable rent to
a family on the housing list with special needs.
 
Option (a) was dismissed owing to its location
to a cemetery.
Option (b) was dismissed owing to the need to
preserve the amenity and tranquillity of the cemetery.
 

None
topline: The Head of Property & Facilities has decided to appropriate a property for general housing accommodation for persons with special needs.

content:
RESOLVED
 
i)             
That the following neighbourhood plans be formally made as part of
the statutory development plan for Horsham District:

 
a)
Cowfold Neighbourhood Plan (2019 – 2031)
b)
Itchingfield Neighbourhood Plan (2015 – 2031)
c)
Lower Beeding Neighbourhood Plan (2014 – 2031)
d)
Pulborough Neighbourhood Plan (2015 – 2031)

 
ii)            
That authority be delegated to the Director of Place, in
consultation with the Cabinet Member for Planning and
Infrastructure and with the consent of the relevant parish council,
to modify any of the above-mentioned neighbourhood plans
(i) for the purpose of correcting
errors or (ii) if the modification does not materially affect the
policies in the plan.
 
 
REASONS
 
i)             
To meet the requirements of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase
Act 2004 and the Neighbourhood Planning (General) Regulations
2012.

 
ii)            
To enable corrections and non-material modifications to be made to
the plans in a timely manner, to ensure the accuracy and
effectiveness of the plans.
 

 
 
ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED BUT REJECTED AS
IDENTIFIED IN THE REPORT
 
The Council could decide not to make one of
the neighbourhood plans if it considered that doing so would
breach, or would otherwise be incompatible with, an assimilated
obligation (previously known as retained EU law) or any of the
Convention rights within the meaning of the Human Rights Act 1998.
Having taken into account the views of the examiners and having
regard to the wider legal implications set out in section 8 of this
report, it is not considered that this is the case. The Council was
therefore required to make the plans.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to formally make several neighbourhood plans as part of the statutory development plan for Horsham District.
